scene.bubble: The final debate! Reflect on the year, learn discourse markers for debating, and speak with confidence.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 6, the finale of Inspiring Nordic. The class holds a formal debate and looks back on a year of growth. In this unit you read about our closing debate, you learn discourse markers that make a discussion flow (on balance, having said that, all in all), and you prepare for Speaking Part 4. This year gave us a voice — let's use it well.

activities.title: Reading — the debate that ended our year

data.title: The debate that ended our year
data.author: mateo
data.text:
Our Inspiring Nordic year ended with a formal debate. The motion was simple but sharp: “This house believes that practical trades matter as much as university degrees.” For weeks we had researched, argued and rehearsed. Now it was real.

Sofía opened for the proposal. She spoke calmly, using the phrases we had practised: “On balance, the evidence is clear.” Liam, on the opposing side, was quick and clever. “Having said that,” he replied, “not every job needs a workshop.” The audience leaned forward.

What impressed our teacher was not who won, but how we spoke. A year ago, most of us were nervous. Now Nadia, once the quietest in the class, delivered a rebuttal that silenced the room. “All in all,” she concluded, “a society that respects every kind of work is a stronger society.”

I acted as moderator, keeping time and calm. It was harder than speaking. You must listen to both sides, concede good points fairly, and never take over.

When the vote came, the room was almost split — which felt right. The best debates rarely have easy answers. Looking back, the project gave us more than grammar and vocabulary. It gave us a voice. And a voice, used well, can change a small part of the world.

Liam, on the opposing side, replied, having said that, not every job needs a workshop. What impressed our teacher was not who won, but how we spoke. Nadia, once the quietest in the class, delivered a rebuttal that silenced the room. I acted as moderator, keeping time and calm. The project gave us a voice.

data.title: Discourse markers for debating
data.intro: Discourse markers organise a discussion and signal your attitude. In a debate they help you concede a point, balance ideas, or sum up. They make you sound fluent and controlled — exactly what Speaking Part 4 rewards.

examples.text: On balance, the evidence supports the trades.
Having said that, not every job needs a workshop.
All in all, it was a fair debate.
That said, we should still respect degrees.

rules: Use on balance and all in all to weigh arguments or conclude.
Use having said that / that said to concede a point before disagreeing.
Put the marker at the start of your sentence, followed by a comma.

items.sentence: I love the plan. ___, it is expensive.
___, it was the best project of the year.
Degrees are useful. ___, trades are just as valuable.
___, I think we should respect every kind of work.

activities.title: Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first. Use the KEY WORD. Write between two and five words.

items.first: The plan is good, but I admit it is expensive.

activities.title: Use of English Part 2 — open cloze. Write ONE word in each gap.

data.text: A good debate is not about shouting. On {1}, the calmest speaker is often the most convincing. You should listen carefully {2} you can answer the other side. Having said {3}, do not be afraid to disagree. It is the person {4} gives clear reasons who wins respect. All {5} all, a debate teaches you to think {6} your feet.

data.script: Well done, Grade 10 — we have reached the final debate. Here is how it works. The motion is that practical trades matter as much as degrees. One team argues for, the other against. Mateo will be the moderator, keeping time and order. Use the discourse markers we practised: on balance, having said that, all in all. Speak clearly, listen to your opponents, and concede a good point when you hear one. In Speaking Part four, examiners reward exactly this: fluency, respect and confidence. Take a breath, and let your voice be heard.

activities.title: Speaking — a mini-debate. In pairs, then record it.

data.text: In pairs, hold a mini-debate. Model: “On balance, I believe practical skills deserve more respect at school.” 1) This house believes every student should learn a trade — argue for or against. 2) Use one discourse marker in every turn (on balance, having said that, all in all). 3) At the end, concede one good point your partner made. Give reasons and examples, then record your discussion.

homework.prompt: Write a short reflection (8–10 sentences) on the Inspiring Nordic project: what did you learn and how did your English improve? Use at least four discourse markers for debating (on balance, having said that, that said, all in all). Capital letters and full stops!
